The getter now combines process-wide and temporary entries, while add_safe_globals() still writes only process-wide state. This makes the existing save/restore idiom promote temporary entries into permanent, process-wide permissions:

    saved = get_safe_globals()
    try:

        # Work with a different allowlist.
    finally:

[mergebot] Approve held CI after `merge -r` rebases an outside contributor's PR

Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.15.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #199190

`@pytorchbot merge -r` force-pushes the rebased commit, and GitHub holds CI of outside contributors for maintainer approval again. trymerge then sees the held checks and fails the merge (e.g. https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/191324), so the maintainer has to approve CI and re-issue the merge.

tryrebase now takes the merge `--comment-id`. For non-ghstack PRs, if the fetched head is the commit the merge command was issued on (same `get_commit_sha_at_comment` trymerge uses), it approves `action_required` runs of the rebased commit for 60s after the push. Commits pushed after the merge comment are never approved. ghstack PRs are unaffected since their authors have write access. Approval failures are logged and don't fail the rebase.

Authored with an AI assistant.

Test plan:

```
cd .github/scripts
python -m pytest test_tryrebase.py
lintrunner .github/scripts/tryrebase.py .github/scripts/test_tryrebase.py .github/workflows/trymerge.yml
```

pr_summary:
Separate value index expressions from indexing

Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.15.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #185853

Introduce value_expr as the dtype-honoring form of index_expr for symbolic
expressions that participate in tensor value computation. A pass classifies
index_expr nodes as indexing or value uses by walking backward from value sinks,
then converts value uses to value_expr in-place. On Triton, value_expr
patches the kernel index dtype and casts the result so arithmetic runs at
the correct width (e.g. int64 for arange(dtype=int64)).

In the future, this should also allow us to no-longer have a "per-kernel" index dtype, but correctly strength reduce particular indexing expressions based on which tensors they are used in. 

See, more analysis here https://docs.google.com/document/d/1AdAUkhzd_3qL2SH4kV9AWj2e55yVrNFqbiQP91beQA0/edit?tab=t.0. 

Fixes multiple bugs. Note - most of LOC here is just test changes. happy to simplify tests etc as needed.


Authored with Claude.

cc @voznesenskym @penguinwu @EikanWang @jgong5 @Guobing-Chen @XiaobingSuper @zhuhaozhe @blzheng @wenzhe-nrv @jiayisunx @ipiszy @kadeng @muchulee8 @amjames @chauhang @aakhundov @coconutruben @jataylo
reviewer_comment:
Yes I agree. It doesn't seem like it should be difficult to prophylactically do this?

I guess it's difficult for user code to trigger this, because the `index_expr` has to actually be used in the double context, and you can't directly trigger this in code (I can't for example do an index computation in user code and then use it to index and write it to a tensor, since these all get distinct lowerings.) So that would indicate that someone wrote a lowering that did this? But we should never allow lowerings that do this! What if we just error in this case?
reviewer_principle: Separate address and value uses — Before narrowing index expressions in Inductor, detect expressions used both for addressing and as tensor values. Reject unsupported mixed-use lowerings or represent the uses separately so index-only assumptions cannot change value semantics.

pr_summary:
Support split_group on the fake process group backend

Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.15.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #186290

The "fake" backend (FakeProcessGroup) did not support split_group: the
Python API raised "backend does not support splitting" before doing any
work, and the C++ path was missing several pieces split_group needs.
new_group works on fake because it re-invokes the backend creator and only
seeds sequence numbers for gloo/nccl; split_group instead drives the generic
ProcessGroup::splitGroup machinery, which exercises code paths the fake
backend never implemented.

Reviewing in dependency order:

- FakeProcessGroup gains supportsSplitting() and a split() that returns a
  child FakeProcessGroup whose rank is the position of this rank within the
  sorted subgroup (mirroring ProcessGroupNCCL::split), or nullptr when this
  rank is not a member.
- setSequenceNumberForGroup()/getSequenceNumberForGroup() are overridden as
  no-ops; split_group unconditionally seeds a sequence number on the child,
  whereas the base Backend implementation throws.
- The FakeProcessGroup constructor coalesces a null Options to a fresh one.
  init_process_group passes pg_options=None to the creator, so the default
  fake PG had a null options_; ProcessGroup::splitGroup dereferences
  getBackendOptions() and would otherwise crash.
- FakeProcessGroup.Options gains __copy__/__deepcopy__, since split_group
  does copy.deepcopy(parent_backend.options).
- FakeStore is reimplemented in C++ (FakeStore.hpp) as a no-op store and
  re-exported from torch.testing._internal.distributed.fake_pg. split_group
  clones the parent store, and the process group holds the store only at the
  C++ level; a pure-Python Store.clone() override is garbage collected once
  the caller drops its reference, so clone() must be a real C++ method.

For the store, subclassing HashStore (which has a real clone()) and stubbing
the methods in Python were both considered. The former turns the fake store
into a functional KV store; the latter does not fix clone()'s lifetime
problem. A dedicated C++ no-op store avoids both issues.

Test Plan:

```
python -m pytest test/distributed/test_fake_pg.py -q
```

New tests cover split rank assignment (an interleaved, unsorted split so the
child rank cannot coincide with the parent rank, cross-checked with
get_global_rank), non-member ranks returning None, and split working when the
caller does not retain the store. Also ran the other fake-store users:

```
python -m pytest test/distributed/test_device_mesh.py -q -k fake_pg
python -m pytest test/distributed/test_collective_utils.py -q
```

Authored by Claude.

reviewer_principle: Check semantic conflicts after rebasing — When extending a C++ backend, reconcile changed base-class interfaces with current main and remove overrides or branches that have become dead code, even when the textual merge succeeds.

pr_summary:
nn/utils: skip no-op .to(first_device) in _get_total_norm

Towards #133586. Replaces #184072 (accidentally closed; the branch was force-pushed afterwards so it cannot be reopened, and its history had no common ancestor with main after a shallow-clone push).

## Summary

For N gradient tensors, the final norm aggregation in `_get_total_norm` always runs `[norm.to(first_device) for norm in norms]`, dispatching N Python method calls that do no data movement in the overwhelmingly common case where all gradients live on one device. This gates the comprehension on an O(k) check over the already-computed device groups (k = unique device/dtype groups, typically 1-3).

For 2000 tensors of 512 elements on CPU (the regime from #133586): `get_total_norm` median 2.45ms -> 2.11ms (~14% faster, M3 Max).

## Why the flat-cat path from #184072 is dropped

While replanting the branch I re-validated the second optimization from #184072 (single `vector_norm` over `torch.cat` of small tensors) and found it loses accuracy versus the hierarchical norm-of-per-tensor-norms reduction: for 2000x512 float32 tensors, relative error vs a float64 reference is **3.1e-5 (flat-cat) vs 4.2e-8 (current foreach path)** — a user-visible numerics change in `clip_grad_norm_`, so it's gone. Only the dispatch-overhead fix remains, which is bitwise-neutral.

All review feedback from #184072 is incorporated: tests live in `test/test_nn.py` on `TestNNDeviceType` (`test_clip_grad_norm_skip_to_single_device`). cc @janeyx99

pr_summary:
fix(nn.utils.prune): don't crash adding a method to an empty PruningContainer

## Summary

`PruningContainer` crashes when built incrementally. `__init__` only assigns `self._tensor_name` in the single-method branch (`PruningContainer(method)`); for an empty container — `PruningContainer()` followed by `add_pruning_method(...)` — `_tensor_name` is never set, so `add_pruning_method` raises `AttributeError: 'PruningContainer' object has no attribute '_tensor_name'` at the `self._tensor_name != method._tensor_name` check.

This empty-then-add pattern is real and in-tree: `global_unstructured` does

```python
container = PruningContainer()
container._tensor_name = "temp"  # to make it match that of `method`
...
container.add_pruning_method(method)
```

and the existing tests do the same `container._tensor_name = "..."` dance. Both only work because they manually assign `_tensor_name` to paper over the missing initialization.

## Fix

`add_pruning_method` now reads the name via `getattr(self, "_tensor_name", None)`: the first method added to an as-yet-unnamed container fixes the name, and later methods must still match it (raising `ValueError` on a mismatch, as before). Once a name is set, behavior is unchanged. No `_tensor_name` is assigned `None`, so the attribute's type is untouched.

This makes building a container incrementally work without the manual workaround.

## Test

Added `test_pruning_container_add_to_empty_adopts_tensor_name`: create `PruningContainer()` with no args, add a method **without** manually setting `_tensor_name`, assert the name is adopted and the method is stored, a second matching method is accepted, and a mismatched one still raises `ValueError`. Before the fix this test errors with `AttributeError` on the first `add_pruning_method`.

```
pytest test/nn/test_pruning.py -k add_to_empty_adopts_tensor_name
```

I was not able to run the suite locally (no compiled `torch` build in my environment). I verified the control-flow change with a standalone reduction of `__init__` / `add_pruning_method` (stubbed method objects, no torch): before the fix, `PruningContainer()`-then-add and the multi-arg `PruningContainer(m1, m2)` form both raise `AttributeError`; after the fix both succeed, single-method construction is unchanged, and a name mismatch still raises `ValueError`. Relying on CI to run the added test against a real build.
reviewer_comment: I think the test for multi-arg is missing PruningContainer(m1, m2) ?
reviewer_principle: Exercise multi-input entry points — When changing container construction, test the form that accepts multiple arguments, not just repeated insertion or single-argument construction.
severity_reason: A missing test of a supported constructor path.

pr_summary:
[not for land] CODA backward epilogue fusion prototype

**Not for land — RFC / prototype.**

A UX prototype for CODA-style backward epilogue fusion across `autograd.Function`
nodes (see "CODA: Rewriting Transformer Blocks as GEMM-Epilogue Programs",
arXiv:2605.19269).

## Problem
The backward of an `autograd.Function` isn't self-contained: for a chain
`mm -> epilogue -> mm`, the epilogue's backward wants to fuse as the epilogue of
the *next* matmul's backward (`grad_a = (grad_c @ W^T) * f'(a)` is a matmul with a
pointwise epilogue), which a single Function can't express since its backward runs
inside one node.

## Approach
The user writes a "1-to-many" op that decomposes into two autograd nodes (a matmul
node + an epilogue marker node) plus a fusion rule. Before backward,
`apply_epilogue_fusion()` walks the graph and arms each matmul node to defer its
activation gradient into the previous epilogue's backward. No graph rewriting:
deferral rides a placeholder grad along the existing edge, and the consumer
epilogue runs the user's fused kernel.

## Files (top-level; the prototype lives out of tree)
- `coda_backward_epilogue_fusion.py` — framework + example ops (MMRelu, MMTanh)
- `coda_backward_epilogue_fusion_test.py` — device-generic numerics + planner tests

## Test plan
```
python coda_backward_epilogue_fusion.py
python coda_backward_epilogue_fusion_test.py
```
Demo + 30 tests pass (CPU and CUDA). Coverage: fused backward matches eager
autograd, the activation grad fuses while the weight grad stays local,
shape-changing epilogues (GLU), branching / missing-rule bail-outs, and a
reference-cycle leak check.

Authored with the assistance of an AI coding assistant (Claude).
reviewer_comment:
You either need:
- assert defer_input_idx == 0
- Have this rule take a grad_input_idx
reviewer_principle: Make gradient-position assumptions explicit — A fusion or deferred-gradient callback must receive the gradient input index it uses, or assert the supported index. Do not silently assume the deferred gradient is at position zero.
severity_reason: The callback must guard or support a nonzero deferred gradient position. This is a substantive correctness requirement for the fusion prototype; its demonstrated examples use position zero.

pr_summary:
Add torch.autograd.graph.node_creation_hook

Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.14.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #189284

Adds a public context manager that registers a thread-local hook fired
once for every autograd Node created within it, with the freshly created
Node as argument. This gives users a creation-time dual of
saved_tensors_hooks: the hook can inspect the node, record it, stash
entries in node.metadata, or register backward pre/post hooks on it.

The motivating use case is attributing backward-pass memory allocations
to the forward region that created the graph: capture TLS state (e.g.
torch.cuda.memory._set_memory_metadata) at node creation and restore it
around the node's execution via register_prehook/register_hook. More
generally it subsumes ad-hoc seq_nr-range bookkeeping for identifying
"all nodes created in a region", and unlike that approach it composes
with create_graph double-backward and checkpoint recomputation because
the TLS rides at::ThreadLocalState onto engine worker threads.

Design notes, in review order:

- aten/src/ATen/NodeCreationHooks.{h,cpp}: TLS stack of SafePyObject
  hooks plus an is_firing reentrancy guard, mirroring SavedTensorHooks;
  lives in ATen so ThreadLocalState can snapshot it.
- torch/csrc/autograd/node.h, function.cpp: fire_node_creation_hooks
  fires at node-attachment time, not in the Node constructor: at
  construction no owning intrusive_ptr exists yet, so the node cannot
  be safely wrapped in a PyObject, and next_edges aren't wired. A
  per-node fired flag makes multi-output nodes fire once.
- torch/csrc/autograd/variable.cpp: impl::set_gradient_edge is the
  single funnel covering codegen ops, custom Functions (C++ and Python
  both go through _wrap_outputs), in-place rebase, and CopySlices. The
  lazy AsStridedBackward0 regeneration in VariableHooks::grad_fn
  assigns grad_fn_ directly and gets an explicit call. AccumulateGrad
  nodes are created lazily in backward and intentionally do not fire.
- torch/csrc/autograd/engine.h, python_engine.{h,cpp}: libtorch_cpu
  cannot call into Python, so firing dispatches through a new
  Engine::call_node_creation_hook virtual overridden by PythonEngine
  (same pattern as get_default_saved_variable_hooks), which takes the
  GIL and wraps the node via functionToPyObject.
- torch/autograd/graph.py, init.cpp, pyi, docs: public context manager
  and bindings modeled on saved_tensors_hooks.

Test Plan:

New tests in test/test_autograd.py cover: per-node firing with node
identity, multi-output nodes firing once, nesting (outermost first),
custom Functions, in-place ops, lazy view grad_fn regeneration, no
firing outside the context, AccumulateGrad not firing, propagation to
create_graph double-backward and checkpoint recomputation via
ThreadLocalState, hook exceptions propagating to the forward op,
reentrancy (ops inside a hook don't recurse), and the backward
pre/post-hook attribution pattern.

```
python test/test_autograd.py -k node_creation_hook -v
python test/test_autograd.py TestAutograd
python test/test_autograd.py TestMultithreadAutograd
```

All pass (399 tests in TestAutograd, 12 new). Also smoke-tested under
torch.compile: hooks fire for nodes created during Dynamo tracing plus
the final CompiledFunctionBackward, consistent with saved_tensors_hooks
behavior under compile.

Authored with Claude Code.
reviewer_comment: It should propagate to any worker thread from any systems.
reviewer_principle: Propagate hook state through shared TLS — Autograd hook registration state must participate in ATen thread-local state propagation so any subsystem's worker threads inherit it, not just one engine's threads.
severity_reason: The requested propagation contract spans thread-creation mechanisms.

saved_tensors_hooks: the hook can inspect the node, record it, stash
entries in node.metadata, or register backward pre/post hooks on it.

with create_graph double-backward and checkpoint recomputation because

after all tensors saved for backward have been stored on it -- so a hook
that inspects the node sees its complete saved state. Firing therefore
happens at the tail of each node-attachment path rather than from a
single funnel inside impl::set_gradient_edge, which runs before saved

  fires at node-attachment time, not in the Node constructor: at
  construction no owning intrusive_ptr exists yet, so the node cannot
  be safely wrapped in a PyObject, and next_edges aren't wired. Every
  attachment path fires a node exactly once by construction, so the

  rather than a runtime dedup.

  the passed-in function -- so callers fire hooks on the composed outer
  node, never the inner one it wraps.

  path captures rebase_history's return so the hook sees the CopySlices
  node; the foreach path fires once per grad_fn after the loop.

New tests in test/test_autograd.py cover: per-node firing with node

pr_summary:
Validate kernel_size matches weight dims in slow_conv_transpose3d

Fixes #142457

## Summary

`slow_conv_transpose3d` accepts `kernel_size` as an explicit argument separate from the weight tensor. When these disagree (e.g. `kernel_size=[1,1,1]` but weight has spatial dims `[2,3,2]`), the columns buffer is allocated using `kernel_size` while the GEMM uses `weight.sizes()`, causing a buffer size mismatch that leads to memory corruption ("double free or corruption" / abort).

This adds a `TORCH_CHECK` in both the CPU and CUDA `slow_conv_transpose3d_shape_check` functions to validate that `kernel_size` matches `weight.size(2:4)`, raising a clear error instead of crashing. This mirrors the existing check in `DepthwiseConv3d`.

## Changes

- `aten/src/ATen/native/NaiveConvolutionTranspose3d.cpp` — add kernel_size vs weight spatial dims check
- `aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/NaiveConvolutionTranspose3d.cu` — same check for CUDA path
- `test/nn/test_convolution.py` — add test calling `aten.slow_conv_transpose3d` with mismatched kernel_size

## Test plan

The new test `test_slow_conv_transpose3d_kernel_size_mismatch` calls `torch.ops.aten.slow_conv_transpose3d` with the exact inputs from the issue (kernel_size `[1,1,1]` vs weight spatial `[2,3,2]`) and asserts a `RuntimeError` is raised instead of crashing.

[ROCm] Fix Python 3.15 manywheel build: resolve numpy source build against target Python

## Summary

The nightly **ROCm** `py3_15` / `py3_15t` manywheel binary builds fail in `.ci/manywheel/build_install_deps.py` while building **numpy from source** (Python 3.15 has no numpy wheels on any index yet, so a source build is unavoidable). numpy's meson build resolves its `python3` dependency via **pkg-config**, and the manylinux ROCm image carries the distro's system `python3-devel` (Python 3.6) on pkg-config's default search path:

```
Determining dependency 'python3' with pkg-config
`pkg-config --cflags python3` -> -I/usr/include/python3.6m
`pkg-config --libs   python3` -> -L/usr/lib64 -lpython3.6m
Run-time dependency python3 found: YES 3.6
sanity_check_for_cython.c:23:6: error: #error Cython requires Python 3.8+.
```

This runs before the target env is created, so **all** ROCm py3.15 jobs fail identically. The **XPU py3.15 builds pass** — that image has no stray system `python3.pc`, so the same numpy source build resolves the correct interpreter and succeeds (pip `-q` is silent on success, which is why the XPU log shows no numpy build).

## Fixes

1. **`prefer_target_python_pkgconfig()`** — prepend the target interpreter's own `pkgconfig` dir to `PKG_CONFIG_PATH` so `pkg-config python3` resolves the CPython we're building for instead of the image's system 3.6 (pkg-config searches `PKG_CONFIG_PATH` before its default libdir). The same guard is added to `build_common.sh`.
2. **`numpy_pin()` bug** — `"cp315".startswith("cp31")` is `True`, so 3.15 was wrongly bucketed to `numpy==2.1.0`, which predates 3.15 and cannot build for it. Switched to numeric `(major, minor)` comparison and added a `cp315 -> 2.5.1` pin (2.5.1 builds on 3.15). Mirrored in `build_common.sh`'s `case`.

## Test plan

- Re-run the ROCm `manywheel-py3_15-rocm*` / `py3_15t-rocm*` binary builds; the numpy source build should resolve `/opt/python/cp315-cp315` and compile.
- Existing Pythons are unaffected: the pkg-config prepend is a no-op where the correct `python3.pc` already resolves, and `numpy_pin()` returns the same values for 3.10–3.14 as before (3.13 -> 2.1.0, 3.14 -> 2.3.4).

bugfix: check_linker_flag cache-variable reuse

`check_linker_flag(LANG FLAGS VAR)` stores its result in `VAR` as a cache variable (see [CheckLinkerFlag](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/module/CheckLinkerFlag.html)). On any later call where VAR already exists in the cache, CMake short-circuits and skips the actual linker probe, reusing the previous verdict.

I discovered this while trying to use LLD linker on AArch64. It kept failing on `--stub-group-size=0x2000000` which if the logic worked properly shouldn't have been applied by CMake to the linker command. It was applied because the `_supported` var was cached from the previous call to `check_linker_flag`.

This commit changes the `add_link_options_if_supported` (which calls `check_linker_flag`) to take a variable name from the user.

CMake now prints this when it encounters an unsupported flag:
```
CMake Warning at cmake/public/utils.cmake:553 (message):
  Attempted to use unsupported link option : --stub-group-size=0x2000000.
```

pr_summary:
inductor: Fall back to ATen for torch.cat with symbolic non-leading dims

Fixes #189940

## Description
When the concatenation dimension of `torch.cat` is a runtime symint (i.e., a non-leading dim is marked dynamic), Inductor lowers it to a fused `pointwise_cat` kernel. This generates per-element indexing containing modulo/division by a runtime symint (`xindex % ks0`, `xindex // ks0`). GPUs cannot strength-reduce division by a runtime value, making the compiled kernel severely ALU-bound and ~2-2.5x slower than the eager ATen execution on hardware like H100.

**What changed:**
* Added a new config flag `fallback_dynamic_cat` (default `True`).
* Modified `cat` lowering in `torch/_inductor/lowering.py` to route the operation to the ATen fallback handler whenever a non-leading dimension is symbolic. 
* Added a regression test `test_dynamic_cat_non_leading_dim_fallback` to ensure correct behavior with dynamic shapes.

This avoids the expensive symbolic `int64` div/mod in the generated Triton kernel, restoring the bandwidth-bound performance. Local benchmarking confirms the compiled execution time is now on par with eager mode.

## Testing
* Passed local linting (`lintrunner -a`).
* Passed `pytest test/inductor/test_torchinductor_dynamic_shapes.py -k "test_dynamic_cat_non_leading_dim_fallback"` on both CUDA and CPU.

The [CUDA 13.4](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/developer-preview/13.4/cuda-toolkit-release-notes/index.html) adds support for the NVIDIA Rubin Architecture (compute capability 10.7).

This PR add some `sm_107` to various places, so PyTorch is Rubin aware.

**Important**: we do not need to specifically compile with `sm_107` arch flag for the releases, since `sm_107` instructions are compatible with `sm_100` (just like `sm_103`).

cc @voznesenskym @penguinwu @EikanWang @jgong5 @Guobing-Chen @XiaobingSuper @zhuhaozhe @blzheng @wenzhe-nrv @jiayisunx @ipiszy @kadeng @muchulee8 @amjames @chauhang @aakhundov @coconutruben @jataylo

Requesting changes — two correctness issues. (The `sm_107`/Rubin premise itself checks out; note at the bottom.)

### 1. `torch/_inductor/codegen/cutlass/utils.py` — `_gen_ops_cached` clobbers `manifest_arch`, regressing SM103

```python
gen_arch = "100" if arch == "103" or arch == "107" else arch
manifest_arch = "103a" if arch == "103" else gen_arch
manifest_arch = "107a" if arch == "107" else gen_arch   # <- unconditionally reassigns
```

The third line reassigns `manifest_arch` in its `else` branch for every non-`107` arch, discarding the `103a` set on the line above. For `arch == "103"`:

1. `gen_arch = "100"`
2. `manifest_arch = "103a"`
3. `arch != "107"` → `manifest_arch = gen_arch = "100"`

So SM103 ends up with `manifest_arch = "100"` instead of `"103a"`, which defeats the arch-conditional-kernel skipping that the adjacent comment says is required ("the CUTLASS manifest must keep the 103a feature arch so unsupported arch-conditional kernels are skipped").     manifest_arch = f"{arch}a"

if(CUDA_VERSION VERSION_GREATER "13.4")

pr_summary:
Raise UnpicklingError on malformed input in weights_only unpickler (#127525)

## Summary

Fixes #127525. `torch.load(..., weights_only=True)` uses the restricted unpickler in `torch/_weights_only_unpickler.py`. On a corrupted or truncated checkpoint, several opcode handlers in the dispatch loop assume a well-formed stack/stream and leak low-level exceptions instead of a clean `UnpicklingError`:

- **Stack underflow** — e.g. `TUPLE3` does `self.stack[-3:] = [(self.stack[-3], ...)]`, raising `IndexError` on an under-full stack (this is the exact traceback in the issue). Same for `TUPLE1/2`, `REDUCE`, `BUILD`, `SETITEM(S)`, `APPEND(S)`, `NEWOBJ`, etc.
- **Truncated fields** — `unpack("<i", read(4))` etc. raise `struct.error` when fewer bytes remain.
- **Dangling memo reference** — `BINGET`/`LONG_BINGET` do `self.memo[idx]`, raising `KeyError`.
- **Undecodable strings** — `GLOBAL`/`SHORT_BINSTRING` decoding raises `UnicodeDecodeError`.

These leak out of `torch.load(weights_only=True)` as `IndexError`/`struct.error`/`KeyError`, which callers loading untrusted files cannot reasonably anticipate or catch.

## Fix

Wrap the opcode-dispatch loop (extracted into `_load()`) so structural corruption is surfaced as `UnpicklingError` — a single, catchable, `pickle`-consistent error type — while re-raising with `from e` to preserve the original traceback:

```python
def load(self):
    try:
        return self._load()
    except (IndexError, _struct_error, KeyError, UnicodeDecodeError) as e:
        raise UnpicklingError("Encountered malformed pickle data ...") from e
```

This mirrors what CPython's C `_pickle` implementation does for a restricted loader on untrusted input (fail-clean). **No security logic changes** — the allowlist/blocklist/`GLOBAL`/`REDUCE`/`BUILD` checks are untouched, so this cannot loosen `weights_only` protections.

## Test

Adds `TestSerialization.test_weights_only_unpickler_malformed_input`:
- Asserts `UnpicklingError` for three malformed payloads: `TUPLE3` stack-underflow (the reported case), a truncated `BININT`, and a dangling `BINGET` memo reference.
- Asserts a well-formed payload still loads correctly — verifying the guard does not over-broadly mask legitimate opcode handling.

## Verification

Confirmed against the reported failure and the legitimate `REDUCE` execution path (e.g. `torch.Size`) loads unchanged, so the guard does not mask errors from allowlisted functions.

## AI Disclosure

Used an AI assistant to help map the vulnerable opcode handlers and draft the change and tests; I reviewed every line, verified the behavior change against the reported crash and legitimate load paths, and confirmed no security check was altered.
reviewer_comment: There can actually be geniune reconstruction errors here as well right? Can we update the language to keep that in mind?
reviewer_principle: Describe deserialization failures honestly — weights_only loading diagnostics must account for genuine reconstruction failures as well as rejected globals or policy restrictions; do not suggest one cause or remedy for every exception.
severity_reason: A misleading diagnostic can direct users to the wrong recovery action.

pr_summary:
[Stable ABI] Add aoti_torch_mps_set_arg_bytes to the MPS shim.

Fixes #190726

Adds `aoti_torch_mps_set_arg_bytes` to the AOTI MPS shim.

The AOTI MPS shim currently exposes only `set_arg_tensor` and `set_arg_int`, so any other non-tensor kernel argument (float/bool scalars, packed structs, small typed arrays) has to be smuggled through a 1-element tensor. Every `setArg` variant in ATen compiles down to either a buffer bind (covered by `set_arg_tensor`) or a byte copy. This function exposes the byte-copy primitive, so the setter surface should not need to grow again for future argument types.

## Benchmark
I ran the same Metal kernel with identical inputs, the only difference was how three non-tensor args (a float scalar, a bool scalar, and a float[2] array) were bound.

| binding path | us/launch |
|---|---|
|`set_arg_bytes` (this PR), bound inline | 6.55 |
| `new_empty` + `fill_` per scalar (the workaround) | 10.42 |

~3.9 us/launch saved (**~1.3 us/scalar, ~1.6x**).

<details>
<summary>Benchmark script</summary>

```python
import time, torch
import torch_test_cpp_extension.mps as mps_ext

SIZE, N_WARMUP, N_TIMED, N_SCALARS = 1000, 200, 2000, 3
scale, negate, low, high = 2.0, True, -0.75, 0.75
x = torch.randn(SIZE, device="mps", dtype=torch.float32)

def path_a_set_arg_bytes():          # scalars bound inline via the new shim
    return mps_ext.get_mps_scale_negate_clamp_output(x, scale, negate, low, high)

def path_b_tensor_workaround():      # pre-shim: new_empty + fill_ per scalar, per launch
    torch.empty(1, device="mps", dtype=torch.float32).fill_(scale)
    torch.empty(1, device="mps", dtype=torch.bool).fill_(negate)
    torch.empty(2, device="mps", dtype=torch.float32).fill_(high)
    return mps_ext.get_mps_scale_negate_clamp_output(x, scale, negate, low, high)

def bench(fn):
    for _ in range(N_WARMUP):
        fn()
    torch.mps.synchronize()
    start = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(N_TIMED):
        fn()
    torch.mps.synchronize()
    return (time.perf_counter() - start) / N_TIMED * 1e6  # us/launch

# Both paths must agree with eager before the timings mean anything.
expected = (x * scale * (-1.0 if negate else 1.0)).clamp(low, high)
torch.testing.assert_close(path_a_set_arg_bytes(), expected)
torch.testing.assert_close(path_b_tensor_workaround(), expected)

a, b = bench(path_a_set_arg_bytes), bench(path_b_tensor_workaround)
print(f"A  set_arg_bytes (this PR)   {a:8.2f} us/launch")
print(f"B  new_empty + fill_         {b:8.2f} us/launch")
print(f"saved: {b - a:.2f} us/launch  ({(b - a) / N_SCALARS:.2f} us per bound scalar)")
print(f"speedup: {b / a:.2f}x")
```

</details>

## New Test Added

`test_mps_set_arg_bytes` in [test/test_cpp_extensions_aot.py](https://github.com/adabeyta/pytorch/blob/17dd274f0d75972e3e562440253c4d5b41f38d3f/test/test_cpp_extensions_aot.py#L113-L127) drives a Metal kernel through the shim from [test/cpp_extensions/mps_extension.mm](https://github.com/adabeyta/pytorch/blob/17dd274f0d75972e3e562440253c4d5b41f38d3f/test/cpp_extensions/mps_extension.mm#L83-L1+57),binding a float scalar, a bool scalar, and a `float[2]` array via `aoti_torch_mps_set_arg_bytes` and checking numerics against eager:

```
python test/run_test.py -i test_cpp_extensions_aot_ninja -- -k test_mps_set_arg_bytes
```

but separately, could we have this live in torch/csrc/stable/c/shim.h actually? with a comment to look here for the other set_args?

* #191020
* __->__ #191019

Python-authored CUDA kernels (e.g. the DSL overrides in torch/_native) need
to implement RNG ops that draw from the same Philox stream as aten's eager
kernels: reserve a chunk of the stream, get (seed, offset), advance the
generator. That primitive exists in C++ as
CUDAGeneratorImpl::philox_cuda_state(increment) but has no Python exposure;
the closest is the inductor-private inductor_reserve_rng_state dispatcher op.

Generator._philox_cuda_state(increment) returns (seed, offset, intragraph)
as three 1-element int64 tensors; kernels consume (seed, offset +
intragraph). Tensors rather than ints so the same code is CUDA-graph-safe:
during capture, seed/offset are the generator's per-capture extragraph
tensors, which replay_prologue refills on every replay — a kernel that loads
them at run time needs no capture-specific plumbing. Reservation semantics
(increment rounded up to a multiple of 4, offset % 4 invariant) match every
other philox_cuda_state caller.

Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.15.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #191999
* #191944

Adds a second way for mark_kernels to discover which nodes a scope contains, on
top of the shared subscriber-callback registry: a RESOURCE / GRAPHNODE_CREATED
handler records each node against whatever scope is open when CUPTI announces
its creation. Selected via torch.cuda.graph(annotation_config={"backend": ...}),
which defaults to "auto" -- CUPTI when the monitor already holds a subscription,
and otherwise today's dependent-edge walk, unchanged.

Two measured limitations of the walk motivate the new backend. First, a scope
entered while the *current* stream is not yet capturing records nothing at all. Second, the walk rescans a nested scope's nodes
once per enclosing scope, so its cost is quadratic in nesting depth where
CUPTI's is linear: at depth 16 over ~2550 nodes, annotation overhead is 73.6ms
against 33.5ms, isolated from the 18.2ms the capture itself costs.

This also folds the capture-graph-id read into one place. #191845 added
maybe_stamp_capture_root at capture_begin for its conditional-body checks, while
maybe_stamp_capture_graph_id read the same id again at capture_end for the
remap. The template graph keeps one id for its whole life, so the capture_end
read is gone and the capture_begin one stamps the graph object as well. 

Review in dependency order: _graph_annotations.py first (the ambient scope
stack, the backend switch, and the unified stamp, all of which the handler
reads), then the new _graph_node_callbacks.py, then the config parsing and
arm/disarm wiring in graphs.py, and finally has_live_subscription() in
monitor.py -- a probe that deliberately does not construct the monitor, since
constructing it would take a CUPTI subscription and lock kineto out for the rest
of the process.

- The single-threaded-autograd requirement gates
only the CUPTI backend rather than enable_annotations as a whole: attributing a
node needs the scope open on the thread that created it, so multithreaded
autograd would mis-attribute nodes its engine threads create -- but making that
unconditional would break every existing annotated capture, because
multithreaded autograd is on by default. So "cupti" raises, "auto" falls back to
the walk, and "edge_walk" is untouched. (capture_error_mode is not the right
gate: it scopes capture's safety checks, not which threads contribute nodes.)
- Registration happens before capture_begin and arming after, so that failing to
obtain CUPTI cannot raise with a capture already underway. 
- nodes belonging
to a child-graph or conditional body are dropped rather than recorded: the
exec-graph ids that traces report for body work are announced by no CUPTI
callback at any point, so recording them would produce keys matching nothing.
The handler counts those drops and disarm() warns once with the total, which is
the edge walk's conditional-body warning without its per-scope cost -- and it
reports what was actually lost, so it covers a scope containing a body as well
as one inside it. The count is warned about outside the callback because a
warnings filter can promote warnings to errors, which must not reach CUPTI's C
dispatch.

One ordering subtlety to check while reviewing: _set_annotations_enabled has to
run before capture_begin, because maybe_stamp_capture_root is gated on it, while
the backend is only final after arming, which needs the capture live. Hence the
separate _set_annotation_backend rather than one call carrying both -- with them
combined the stamp silently no-ops and the conditional-body detection from
#191845 stops working, with no test failing loudly.

New tests, including the two that carry the justification above --
test_scope_entered_before_stream_joins_capture (0 annotated under the walk, 3
under CUPTI) and test_parity_with_edge_walk. The forward-compat driver is
required for the graph annotation APIs:

```bash
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/usr/local/cuda-13.2/compat:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH \
  python test/test_cuda_graph_utils.py TestCuptiAnnotationBackend -v
```

11 passed.

Regression coverage, since mark_kernels gained a branch and the capture-id stamp
moved:

```bash
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/usr/local/cuda-13.2/compat:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH \
  python test/test_cuda_graph_utils.py
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/usr/local/cuda-13.2/compat:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH \
  python test/test_cuda.py -k graph
```

test_graph_capture_error_releases_reserved_segments, is pre-existing and not
from this change: it passes in isolation, and clean origin/main reproduces the
identical 141-run/1-failure result.

test_scope_inside_conditional_body_records_nothing passing is the check that the
capture_begin stamp actually fires -- it would fail if the stamp no-opped.

pr_summary:
Introduce public torch.foreach APIs

Big change! This PR is to make our foreach ops more discoverable and legit by making them public.

Design decisions:
- our new foreach ops will live in `torch.foreach`
- `torch.foreach.op` will call `torch._foreach_op`. there is no new ATen op, kernel or codegen.
- they will be behaviorally the same as our private offerings, in fact they are semantically the same in terms of overloads offered, underlying call, everything. EXCEPT we do change some param names to be more consistent and future proof.
- AND we do not offer out variants! The existing out variants for the private offerings aren't true out variants + use more memory.
- our naming scheme: pluralize inputs (as foreach ops require some arg to be listed over) BUT maintain all other logical names (tensor1, weight, end, etc) as those can be either singular or plural.
- `torch._foreach_powsum` is intentionally private, so it is not exposed
- we wanted to keep this change minimally disruptive. we test all our new public foreach ops through the existing OpInfo mechanism + we add one-off tests to ensure that the private + public are compatible still. we do NOT run double the tests.

Invariants I reviewed:
- `_foreach_add` will route to the Tensor alpha overload when an alpha is specified and the Scalar overload when it isn't for a scalar tensor input (matching existing behavior)
- The overload orders match the order set in pythonArgParser
- default params and positionality vs keyword only match private APIs. e.g., `clone(memory_format=None)` and positional `norm(..., dtype)`
- In-place operations return the exact input list or tuple, including under torch.compile
- OpInfo names continue identifying the underlying private ATen operators  (matching aten names) so existing skips and test IDs remain valid + this change is minimal

What I have yet to review but plan to:
- I will spotcheck that the docs look good for each op

[native_aot][4/7] gen_aot_lib: the generated kernel source

Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.16.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #191669
* #190899
* #190898
* #190897
* #194243
* #194242
* #194241
* __->__ #194240
* #194239
* #194238
* #190896

Human note:

Real work! Generate launchers and conditional gating functions in C++ for embedding.

Claude note:

The first half of the generator: a declaration plus its sidecars become the C++
ATen links. Source production only -- the CLI and the emitted CMake are next, so
this reads as "what is generated and why".

gen_op emits one .cpp per declaration: a marshalling launcher per kernel (from the
sidecar kind's Toolchain, so the guard chain is toolchain-blind), an early-out over
the shipped capabilities, then one cond chain per capability ending in `return
false` so the op falls through to aten.

The same declaration also emits a covers() predicate, so the router can ask
whether the AOT path applies without entering it. Its signature comes from
torchgen's structured introspection rather than being written out per op, which is
what makes it the signature aten will really call -- including for an op whose meta
function precomputes arguments.

Two gates are generated rather than written per declaration. The device gate
compares exact major.minor, because sm_103 reports major 10: a major-only gate
offered it sm_100 artifacts and the module load then failed instead of declining,
with no retry. The size gate exists because a kind whose exported ABI narrows
shapes to int32 cannot be handed a dim past INT32_MAX; it is per-kind and
per-argument, the width being a property of that ABI rather than of aten.

Test Plan:

```
pytest tools/test/test_native_aot_tools.py
```

Run at this commit's own tree, in a checkout with no built torch -- which is
what lint.yml's "Test tools" job has. This commit's tests cover the emitted
launchers and per-capability cond chains, the device gate comparing exact
major.minor, the shipped-versus-declared arch selector, the covers() predicate's
signature and the device it reads, and the int32 size gate being per-kind and
per-argument.

pr_summary:
[native_aot][5/7] gen_aot_lib: emitted CMake, the version script, generation ordering

Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.16.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #191669
* #190899
* #190898
* #190897
* #194243
* #194242
* __->__ #194241
* #194240
* #194239
* #194238
* #190896

Human note:

Driver script for generation -- controls how the previous commits are put together
into one cohesive thing. Generates the cmake for libtorch_cuda relinking.

Claude note:

The generator gains a driver, and with it the build integration the previous
commit left out.

native_aot.cmake is not data for CMake to parse -- it IS the CMake calls, so
caffe2/CMakeLists.txt is a single include(... OPTIONAL). An earlier version put
~370 lines of parsing and comparison in CMake, none of it reachable by a test. The
link options are emitted in one exact spelling because each part is load-bearing:
target_link_options de-duplicates, so bare -Xlinker tokens collapse and the link
fails; LINKER: expands to -Wl, which the driver splits on commas; SHELL: splits its
own value on spaces.

Ordering is the correctness argument. The old file is deleted first, sources are
buffered until every declaration has passed its refusals, and the new file is
written atomically and last, so its CONTENT is the only evidence a generation
finished. export.py joins that rule here, invalidating the previous generation
before touching an artifact and on every refusal -- artifacts are direct link
inputs in build.ninja, so an interrupted export plus an ordinary `cmake --build`
relinked a library mixing two source revisions. Invalidation OVERWRITES the
include with its nothing-to-embed form rather than deleting it: CMake registers an
include()d file as a configure dependency only if it existed at configure time, so
a deleted one made the next generation invisible to `cmake --build` and the
kernels stayed out of the library however many times it was rebuilt.

The version script localizes the objects' _mlir_* entry points, which export_to_c
gives default visibility and which would otherwise join torch_cuda's public ABI. A
static torch_cuda cannot take it at all, because CMake silently discards
target_link_options for an archive -- the script would evaporate while appearing to
be applied -- so the verdict in the next commit refuses such a build outright.

Test Plan:

```
pytest tools/test/test_native_aot_tools.py
```

Run at this commit's own tree, in a checkout with no built torch -- which is
what lint.yml's "Test tools" job has. This commit's tests cover the emitted
CMake calls and the opt-out among them, every version-script pattern being
anchored on a kernel prefix and the `local:` directive itself, the delete-first /
buffer-sources / write-last ordering and the atomic write, invalidation leaving an
include a later generation is still seen through, generation scoped to this
build's arch list, and the sidecar-field and orphan-artifact refusals.

Authored with an AI assistant (Claude Code).
reviewer_comment: Would this delete the cmake rather than overriding it as we say we should above?
reviewer_principle: Preserve CMake dependency tracking during invalidation — If CMake includes a generated file and tracks it as a configure dependency, invalidate it by overwriting it with a no-work form rather than deleting it, so later regeneration still triggers reconfiguration.
severity_reason: The original hunk deletes native_aot.cmake despite the overwrite invariant. Author reply 3904827328 confirms the mismatch and fixes it with a nothing-to-embed form; the question conveys a concrete correctness finding.

[native_aot][7/7] build_stage2: relink, patch the wheel, and the build wiring

Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.16.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #191669
* #190899
* #190898
* #190897
* __->__ #194243
* #194242
* #194241
* #194240
* #194239
* #194238
* #190896

Human note:

Finally putting everything together. Relink libtorch_cuda, correctly fixup the wheel, and
make sure everything (paths, manifests, etc.) are all aligned and correct.

Claude note:

The driver on top of the verdict, and the CI and dev flows that call it. With
this commit a standard CUDA build ships embedded AOT kernels.

A post-install step, because the kernel builders package-import torch and
scikit-build-core has no post-build hook inside the PEP 517 backend. It
reconfigures before a targeted relink of torch_cuda: the generated file registers
itself in CMAKE_CONFIGURE_DEPENDS only from the reconfigure that first READS it,
and the build.ninja on disk predates this generation -- without that the relink
silently omitted the kernels (417 MiB where 423 ships).

--wheel patches the relinked library and its RECORD entry back into the built
wheel, so test jobs get the kernels rather than a library replaced only on disk;
released wheels get the same before repair_wheel.py, so it goes through patchelf
like any other. It asserts that torch imports, because a kernel-free release wheel
must fail rather than skip -- and the ASan and TSan images cannot `import torch`
plainly, which is why the CI call is CUDA-guarded.

It assumes the torch it finds installed is the one this tree just built, and
VERIFIES that rather than repairing it: the reconfigure has to report embedding
before anything is relinked, the relinked library has to report its own kernels
before this exits, and a failure past that point says to reinstall. A run that
DECLINES overwrites a native_aot.cmake an earlier one left behind, because the
include is unconditional and the release matrix shares one build tree across eight
interpreters -- so the wheel for an interpreter with no DSL runtime was shipping
the previous interpreter's objects.

caffe2/CMakeLists.txt gets the one include line, EnvVarForwarding.cmake caches
TORCH_NATIVE_AOT so the opt-out survives a reconfigure, and CONTRIBUTING.md states
the skip reasons.

Test Plan:

```
pytest tools/test/test_native_aot_tools.py
```

Run at this commit's own tree, in a checkout with no built torch -- which is
what lint.yml's "Test tools" job has. This commit's tests cover patch_wheel's
RECORD and its ZIP64 metadata -- a copied member must not inherit the source's
stale offsets, which pip and unzip accept and `uv` refuses -- each of main()'s
refusals from the verdict down to a relink that produced no library, the argv and
env contract with both children including the one artifacts directory they share,
and the CI shells and CMake read as text.

PR CI cannot reach the relink at this commit -- no declaration exists yet, so
should_run() reports "nothing declares kernels" in every build job -- so it was
exercised by hand on a clean tree:

```
rm -rf build && USE_CUDNN=1 USE_CUDA=1 USE_MSLK=1 MAX_JOBS=32 spin develop
```

Stage 2 exported all four declarations (54 objects + 4 generated sources, 4.0 MiB),
reconfigured, relinked, copied 324 MiB over the installed torch and passed its
embedded-kernel probe. On that build: test/python_native, one file per process, 331
passed; `test_ops.py -k "cuda and (topk or scatter_add or index_add)"` 115 passed;
test_sort_and_select 207; test_scatter_gather_ops 247; test_indexing 380.

Authored with an AI assistant (Claude Code).
reviewer_comment: Shouldn't we make sure that the exact same cache as the previous build is used here? And nothing is triggering a change in configuration?
reviewer_principle: Preserve build configuration during a second stage — An incremental native-AOT relink must reuse the original build's CMake cache and reject configuration drift caused by environment forwarding before altering the installed library.
severity_reason: The reviewer makes cache preservation blocking, but blocking does not itself establish P0. This is a substantive build-configuration invariant; the comment does not demonstrate a fundamental serious failure requiring the top severity.

pr_summary:
Exclude meta tensors from check_leaked_tensors

## Issue

check_leaked_tensors installs gc.DEBUG_SAVEALL so that everything the collector
reclaims is appended to the module-global gc.garbage rather than freed, then
filters gc.garbage by isinstance(obj, matched_type) to report tensors kept alive
by reference cycles. Two properties of that implementation produce failures that
are unrelated to leaked memory.

First, meta tensors are counted. A meta tensor carries shape, dtype and stride
metadata and owns no storage, so it cannot hold tensor memory alive no matter how
many cycles reference it. The docstring is explicit that the check exists to find
cycles holding a Tensor alive precisely because that is more serious than the
ordinary Python refcycles it intends to ignore - counting meta tensors turns the
report back into exactly the refcycle-hygiene signal it says it ignores.

Second, gc.garbage is module-global and gc.set_debug(0) does not empty it, so
objects saved by one check_leaked_tensors block remain there after the block
exits. The next block's garbage_objs.extend(filter(match_obj, gc.garbage)) then
re-counts them. The warning consequently depends on how many earlier blocks ran
in the same process and on when the collector happened to run, making it
order-dependent across tests sharing an interpreter.

## Summary

Exclude meta tensors from check_leaked_tensors and clear gc.garbage per block.

This filters meta tensors out of match_obj and empties gc.garbage in the `finally`.
Callers that inspect the yielded garbage_objs list are unaffected: it is a
separate list holding its own references, populated before the finally runs, and
it is the documented way to examine results after the block exits. A caller
reading gc.garbage directly afterwards now sees it empty, which is the intended
change - those entries are this block's own DEBUG_SAVEALL byproduct.

Clearing unconditionally rather than snapshotting and restoring prior entries
does mean a nested check_leaked_tensors would lose the outer block's entries.
Nesting is already unsupported, since the inner block's gc.set_debug(0) disables
SAVEALL for the outer one, so this does not regress anything.


## Checklist

- [ ] Passes lint (`spin fixlint`)
- [ ] Added/updated tests
- [ ] Updated documentation (if applicable)
- [ ] Included benchmark results (for PRs impacting perf)

## BC-breaking?

[Inductor][ROCm] Support all input layouts in FlyDSL gfx950 GEMM

## Summary

Extend the FlyDSL gfx950 GEMM template from NT-only input handling to all four layouts:

- NN
- NT
- TN
- TT

The layout is inferred from input strides and propagated through the lowering, heuristics, template parameters, and kernel cache key.

The kernel now:

- Consumes logical `A[M, K]` and `B[K, N]` tensors directly.
- Selects the appropriate leading strides and LDS layouts.
- Uses transposed LDS reads where required.
- Preserves the existing inline-assembly G2S pipeline, K-tail handling, and HTI behavior.
- Adds the required `s_nop 0` after writing M0 on CDNA4.

## Testing

- Added layout-gating tests for NN/NT/TN/TT.
- Added gfx950 end-to-end correctness coverage for all four layouts.

## Performance

Compared current FlyDSL graph-replay performance against the fixed ATen and Triton reference results reported in [#190903](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/190903). The current-run ATen and Triton measurements were not used.
Across the 15 overlapping BF16 NT shapes:
- vs PR Triton: **1.206x** geomean speedup, compared with **1.193x** in the original PR.
- vs PR ATen: **1.165x**, compared with **1.153x**.
- vs the faster PR baseline per shape: **1.115x**, compared with **1.103x**.

Current FlyDSL graph throughput is **1.07% higher geomean** than the FlyDSL results reported in #190903, indicating no aggregate performance regression.

[Testcase Refactoring] Resolve default backend from device in common test base classes

## Motivation

Two common test base classes select process-group backends and devices through
hard-coded CUDA-era paths:

- `ShardedTensorTestBase.with_comms` / `init_pg` default to `"nccl"`, so a
  device-instantiated out-of-tree accelerator class does not use its registered
  default backend unless every call site passes a module-level backend global.
- `DistributedTestBase.backend` maps cuda/hpu/xpu explicitly and sends every
  other device to gloo; `create_pg` then probes the current accelerator even
  though its device is already an argument.

## Changes

`ShardedTensorTestBase`:

- add a `backend` property that resolves the default backend from the injected
  `device_type`, while preserving the previous `"nccl"` default for legacy
  subclasses that have not yet migrated to `instantiate_device_type_tests`;
- add a `current_device` property that returns the unindexed injected device
  while `rank < 0`, and `device_type:rank` in worker processes;
- make `with_comms`, `init_comms`, and `init_pg` default to `backend=None`, with
  `init_pg` resolving `None` through the property while preserving explicit
  backend values;
- keep the `dist.is_backend_available()` admission check and the
  `torch.accelerator.is_available() and backend != dist.Backend.GLOO` rank
  binding as landed by #190528 (a superset of the non-gloo rule this PR
  proposed);
- reduce the wrapper precheck to the effective non-gloo backend and the
  device-count condition. The requested backend is resolved through the
  `backend` property, so a bare `@with_comms` on a device-instantiated class
  is not skipped for `None != default_backend`. The `current_accelerator()`
  probe and the backend-vs-accelerator-default comparison that #190528 carried
  are dropped: once the default backend comes from the instantiated device,
  a mismatch can only come from an explicit hard-coded backend at a call site,
  and that should surface as a failure to fix rather than a silent skip.

`DistributedTestBase`:

- replace the cuda/hpu/xpu/gloo chain with a direct
  `c10d.get_default_backend_for_device(device)` call;
- let `create_pg` accept an explicit backend override and bind non-gloo ranks
  from the injected `device` argument instead of `current_accelerator()`.

The legacy fallback applies only when `device_type` is absent. If a device type
is present but has no registered default backend, the registry lookup still
fails instead of silently selecting another backend.

## Scope

This PR covers only `DistributedTestBase` and `ShardedTensorTestBase`.
`C10dTorchCommsTestBase` is not included: TorchComms has its own backend
availability and registration path, and that work remains coordinated with
#194152 rather than being partially duplicated here.

#190528 (landed as 3476cfd24445) touched the same `ShardedTensorTestBase.init_pg`
/ `with_comms` region; this PR is rebased on top of it. The admission check and
rank binding are the ones #190528 landed; the wrapper precheck follows this
PR's reviewed shape (see Changes) and supersedes the three-part precheck
#190528 carried. #194152 touches the same `DistributedTestBase` region and the
usual rule applies to whichever lands second.

## Behavior

| path | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| explicit `backend=...` | passed through | passed through |
| instantiated bare `@with_comms` | fixed nccl default | resolves from injected `device_type` |
| current rank device | no shared helper | unindexed device before spawn, `device_type:rank` in workers |
| `DistributedTestBase.backend`, cuda/xpu/hpu/cpu | nccl/xccl/hccl/gloo | same values through the registry |
| other registered devices | silently gloo | registered default backend |
| legacy subclass without `device_type` | fixed nccl default | preserves nccl default |
| present but unregistered device type | implicit fallback | explicit lookup error |
| `DistributedTestBase.create_pg` rank binding | nccl/xccl plus a runtime device probe | any non-gloo backend, using the injected device |
| `ShardedTensorTestBase` rank binding | as landed by #190528 | unchanged |
| `with_comms` precheck | accelerator present / backend equals its default / enough devices (#190528) | non-gloo effective backend and enough devices; no accelerator probe |
| explicit non-default backend on an accelerator host (e.g. `nccl` on a non-CUDA device) | skipped | not skipped; `init_pg` / `init_process_group` reports it |

## Test plan

Re-run on the rebased head, stacked on top of the landed #190528 change. The
focused suite contains eight contracts, including an uninstantiated legacy
`ShardedTensorTestBase` assertion:

- NPU: eight focused contracts passed with four HCCL ranks, covering
  default and explicit backends for `DistributedTestBase.create_pg`, an
  instantiated bare `@with_comms` path, and the parent/worker branches of
  `current_device`, plus the missing-`device_type` legacy fallback
  (8 passed, 0 skipped);
- CPU: the same eight contracts passed with gloo, including the bare
  `backend=None` path, both `current_device` branches, and confirmation that
  gloo does not bind an accelerator device (8 passed, 0 skipped);
- both runs asserted the reviewed source shape before executing and restored
  the prepared source tree byte-for-byte afterwards;
- CUDA: nccl resolution and multi-device behavior through CI.
reviewer_principle: Use device-generic distributed backend selection — Select the default process-group backend through dist.get_default_backend_for_device(device) instead of hard-coding a backend mapping in tests.
severity_reason: Uses the established device-to-backend contract.

[inductor] Route compile options to backend-owned ConfigModules via a registry

### Motivation

Out-of-tree Inductor backends can own a `ConfigModule` through `register_backend_for_device(device_custom_config=...)` (#158254), but its options cannot currently be passed through `torch.compile(..., options={...})`.

`_TorchCompileInductorWrapper.apply_options` only validates against `torch._inductor.config`, while `compile_fx` and `get_compiler_config()` also apply patches only to that module. Downstreams such as `torch_npu` therefore monkey-patch `ConfigModule.get_config_copy()` and write private `_ConfigEntry` objects into the core config.

### Proposal

Add an Inductor compile-option registry that maps a user-facing option name to a key in its owning `ConfigModule`:

```python
from torch._inductor.compile_option_registry import register_compile_option

register_compile_option(
    "npu_backend",
    module="torch_npu._inductor.compile_config",
)

torch.compile(fn, options={"npu_backend": "mlir"})
```

Unregistered options continue to use `torch._inductor.config`.

`apply_options` resolves registered routes and type-checks values against the owning module. `compile_fx` splits patches between the core config and routed owner modules. The patch context is re-entered for delayed backward compilation, matching the existing `config.patch(...)(inner_compile)` behavior.

Routed configs used by the current compile are snapshotted and replayed for serialized `compile_fx_ext` compilation. Active routed owner configs are also included in the FX graph cache key.

The option remains owned by the backend module; this does not add `torch._inductor.config.<vendor_key>` attributes.

### Alternatives Considered

- **`ConfigModule.add_config()` (#192299):** Provides a general mechanism for extending an installed `ConfigModule`, while this proposal is scoped to routing Inductor compile options to backend-owned config modules.
- **Routing by device:** `apply_options` runs before a graph or device is known.

This is an alternative to the `ConfigModule.add_config()` approach in #192299 and implements the option-registry direction suggested by @aorenste during its review.

### Test Plan

```bash
python test/inductor/test_compile_option_registry.py -v
python test/inductor/test_config.py -v
```

reviewer_principle: Extend the existing backend interface — Backend compile-option discovery should be a method on the existing backend class rather than a new independent global registry that duplicates ownership.

pr_summary:
Teach the triage skill to flag issues affecting an upcoming release

Has the triage bot flag issues that affect an upcoming release, so they can be found with a search instead of by reading the queue.

## Why

Release-relevant issues are currently surfaced by the release manager reading through incoming issues. Anything missed there tends to be found later — often by a downstream user, sometimes after the RC. Flagging at triage time turns that into:

```
is:issue label:"release triage"
```

## Release triage is continuous, not a branch-window activity

The label means *"whoever owns the release needs to see this"*. What happens next depends on where the cycle is:

- **Between a completed release and the next branch cut** — the fix lands in main and ships in the next release. Flagging early is what keeps the problem from reaching the branch at all.
- **Between branch cut and release** — the fix lands in main and is then cherry-picked, under the [RELEASE.md](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/RELEASE.md) criteria.

Same signal either way; only the remedy differs. The step says this explicitly so the label doesn't get treated as meaningless outside the cherry-pick window.

## Criteria

Add `release triage` when **any** hold:

- regression against the most recent released minor (pair with `module: regression`)
- critical correctness or stability: silent correctness, BC break, crash/segfault, deadlock, large memory leak
- critical fix to a feature introduced in the most recent minor
- binaries / packaging: wheels, conda, Docker, install, the release build (pair with `module: binaries`)
- **would ship broken in the next release** — a defect on main, a nightly, an RC, or the release branch that reaches users if nobody fixes it, including anything surfaced by release validation or downstream canaries. This holds even when it is not a regression against anything, e.g. a bug in code that has never shipped. The other four criteria structurally miss this case, and it is where a lot of real release blockers come from.

Apply generously: a false positive costs one glance, a miss costs a broken release. It is a **flag, not a verdict** — a fix may not exist yet, and whether to cherry-pick is never the bot's call. Independent of `triage review`, so an issue can carry both. Excluded: feature requests, enhancements, docs-only, and regressions against versions older than the last released minor.

## Also

**`labels.json`** gets the label entry. Not documentation — `scripts/validate_labels.py` strips any label not present in that file, so without it the bot would appear to apply `release triage` while the hook silently dropped it every time.

## Prerequisite

The `release triage` label needs to exist on the repo before this does anything; @atalman is creating it.

## Scope

This flags **issues**. The skill only triages issues, so PRs continue through the existing cherry-pick process — the effect is that the issue behind a fix gets flagged, surfacing it before or alongside the PR. Flagging PRs would be a separate change.

`count` in `labels.json` says `284` while the array holds `281` entries (282 after this). Pre-existing drift; left alone rather than folding an unrelated correction into this PR.

---

Filed with the help of Claude Code.
reviewer_comment:
```suggestion

**You are told which version is current — never guess it.** Your prompt carries a
`RELEASE CONTEXT` block giving the most recent released minor version. If the block
says `unknown`, skip the two version-dependent criteria below and judge the rest on their
own merits.
```
reviewer_principle: Use supplied release context — Release-dependent automation must use the version resolved into its prompt or run context, not a hard-coded skill version or model memory. If the supplied version is unknown, skip only the version-dependent criteria.
severity_reason: Prevents stale release assumptions from deciding triage outcomes.

[MPS] Fix compile_shader header resolution in editable installs

Closes #195293

I have built this branch standalone and run its tests locally on Apple silicon before submitting.
The description below was drafted with an AI assistant, so it is quoted rather than presented as my own prose.

> ## Why this is needed
>
> Fixes a broken developer path rather than adding an operator. On any source build (`pip install -e .`), every `#include <c10/metal/...>` inside `torch.mps.compile_shader` fails to resolve, which silently turns 14 tests in `TestMetalLibrary` into errors instead of skips. Anyone working on MPS kernels hits this.
>
> ## Change
>
> `torch.mps.compile_shader` inlines `#include` directives before handing the
> source to the Metal compiler, and it looks for them in exactly one place:
> `torch/include`. That directory only exists in a packaged install. Building
> PyTorch from source with `pip install -e .` never creates it, so every
> `#include <c10/metal/...>` in a shader fails to resolve and the compile dies
> with "file not found".
>
> That is not a niche path. It is what every developer working on MPS kernels
> hits, and it silently disables a chunk of the test suite: on a source build,
> `TestMetalLibrary` loses `test_metal_include`, `test_metal_randn`,
> `test_metal_error_buffer`, `test_metal_compiler_bug_workaround`, the four
> `test_atomic_add_*` cases and the six `test_reduction_utils_*` cases, 14 tests
> in total, all reported as errors rather than skips.
>
> The fix is to also search the source checkout when the headers are visibly
> there, which is the same convention `embed_headers` in
> `torch/utils/_cpp_embed_headers.py` already uses for its own default. The
> repository root and `aten/src` are appended only when `c10/metal` exists next
> to the `torch` package, so a packaged install is unaffected: in site-packages
> that directory does not exist and the search list is unchanged.
> `_embed_headers` already skips include directories that do not resolve, so
> ordering the packaged path first keeps it authoritative where it exists.
>
> Test Plan:
>
> On a `pip install -e .` build, before the change every c10/metal header fails
> to resolve and after it they all do:
>
> ```
> python -c "
> import torch
> for h in ('c10/metal/atomic.h', 'c10/metal/utils.h',
>           'c10/metal/special_math.h', 'c10/metal/random.h',
>           'ATen/native/mps/kernels/Pooling.h'):
>     torch.mps.compile_shader('#include <%s>' % h)
>     print(h, 'OK')
> "
> ```
>
> The 14 tests listed above go from error to passing:
>
> ```
> python test/test_mps.py TestMetalLibrary -v
> python test/test_mps.py -k atomic_add -v
> ```
>
> `TestMetalLibrary` is 19 passed / 3 skipped, and the four `atomic_add` cases
> pass.

Fix an annotation leak on failed capture, and retire the clear_kernel_annotations workflow

Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.17.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #195398
* #195397
* #194854

Three findings from integrating the annotation store into a large trainer.

A capture that completes a mark_kernels scope and then fails in capture_end leaked its
annotations for the life of the process. resolve_pending_annotations has to run before
capture_end, because the rekey inside instantiate() is what consumes what it writes, so
its entries land keyed by the capture graph's id and only instantiate() rewrites them to
an exec id. When capture_end raises there is no exec graph and no rewrite, and
remove_kernel_annotations (the graph-destroy path) matches on exec ids, so nothing could
reach them again. __exit__ now purges that capture's entries when capture_end raises.
The purge is scoped to capture_end alone rather than the whole try block -- once it
returns the capture is usable and its annotations are worth keeping -- and is guarded on
the graph not having been remapped already, since keep_graph=False instantiates inside
capture_end.

An earlier writeup of this suggested moving the resolve into capture_end, after the
capture-id stamp. That no longer applies, and the reason is what makes the simpler fix
work: the stamp now happens at capture_begin, so graph._capture_graph_id is already set
when capture_end fails and we know exactly which entries are ours to drop.

clear_kernel_annotations is deprecated rather than deleted. It has no caller in torch
outside tests, and its docstring recommended clearing "once recorded annotations have
been consumed (e.g. after saving them alongside a profiler trace)" -- the
pickle-alongside-trace flow that inline trace export retires. For a long-running trainer
that advice is actively harmful: graphs are captured once and replayed for the whole run,
so a global wipe discards annotations for graphs that are still live and still being
joined against, and growth is already bounded by the remap on instantiate plus
remove_kernel_annotations on destroy. The docstring separately claimed clearing "revokes
recording from every scope opened before the clear", which is not true -- only backward
brackets are versioned by the generation counter, so a forward scope open across a clear
registers on exit as usual. Both claims are corrected, the second now has a test, and
tests call a new private _reset_kernel_annotations for isolation so the suite does not
trip the warning; the one test that is about the public entry point asserts it.

Cleaning up those call sites also removed the redundant ones: nine tests opened with a
reset that their class fixture already does, and two registry-only classes reset in
tearDown alone, which is why each of their tests began with one -- those now use setUp
plus addCleanup. The resets kept are the ones that do work: between iterations of a
loop, or mid-test where the reset is the thing under test.

Finally, register_capture_end_hook documents that capture-end hooks are best-effort:
skipped entirely when cudaStreamEndCapture raises, and truncated when an earlier hook
raises. A consumer using one for teardown needs its own fallback on the error path.

Test Plan:

```
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/usr/local/cuda-13.2/compat python test/test_cuda_graph_utils.py
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/usr/local/cuda-13.2/compat python test/profiler/test_profiler.py TestPythonChromeTraceExport TestChromeTraceInlineAnnotations
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/usr/local/cuda-13.2/compat python test/profiler/test_cupti_node_timer.py
```

115, 16 and 8 tests pass. test_failed_capture_end_discards_annotations is the regression
test for the leak: reverting just the __exit__ change makes it fail. test_public_bindings
has one failure in this environment that predates the change and is unrelated
(torch.distributed.debug._debug_handlers needs the `tabulate` package).

Authored with assistance from Claude Code.
reviewer_comment: Hmmm. Shouldn't cuda graph exit unwind the stream context? This is it's own problem but seems worth fixing?
reviewer_principle: Unwind stream context on graph-capture failure — CUDA graph context exit must restore the caller's stream even if capture_end raises; do not rely on individual tests or callers to repair leaked stream state.
severity_reason: The hunk shows a test workaround for missing context cleanup.

This changes what the CUDA variant checks, not just the names. `torch.accelerator.get_device_capability()` isn't the same API as `torch.cuda.get_device_capability()`: it returns `{"supported_dtypes": ...}`, not the compute capability. And `torch.accelerator.set_device_index` / `is_available` / `device_count` go through the generic accelerator bindings, not `torch.cuda`. The test exists to check that `torch.cuda.*` behaves the same before and after FakeTensorMode, so with this change the CUDA run no longer covers the functions it was written for.

Line 303 already uses `torch.get_device_module(...)`, which has `get_device_capability`, `set_device`, `current_device`, `is_available` and `device_count` for both cuda and xpu. Using it for all of them keeps the CUDA coverage and still works for XPU:

```python
def accelerator_calls_behavior_unchanged():
    device_mod = torch.get_device_module("{device}")
    ...
        device_mod.get_device_capability()
    ...
        device_mod.set_device(1)
    ...
        device_mod.current_device()
    ...
    assert device_mod.is_available() == False
    assert device_mod.device_count() == 0
```

I tried that version on an XPU box with `ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR=*:cpu`. The three `torch.xpu` calls each raise `No XPU devices are available.`, the count is still 5, and the script passes both before and after the fake mode block.
reviewer_principle: Preserve API coverage when generalizing device tests — A test of backend-module behavior must continue calling that backend module; generic accelerator APIs can have different semantics or bindings. Use torch.get_device_module(device) to select corresponding CUDA or XPU operations without changing what the test verifies.
severity_reason: Explicit API coverage regression and concrete replacement; source reports an XPU check.

reviewer_comment:
`ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR=*:cpu` alone doesn't hide the GPUs from `torch.xpu.is_available()` before lazy init. Before init, `device_count()` counts devices through Level Zero Sysman (`_device_count_zes`), and that path only looks at `ZE_AFFINITY_MASK`. On my 8-device box:

```
ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR=*:cpu                       -> is_available()=True, device_count()=8, importing op_db raises "No XPU devices are available."
ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR=*:cpu ZE_AFFINITY_MASK=""   -> is_available()=False, device_count()=0, op_db imports fine
```

The `op_db` import fails because the SDPA OpInfo evaluates `PLATFORM_SUPPORTS_FLASH_ATTENTION` at import time. That goes through `common_xpu.Xe2_Or_Later`, which calls `get_device_capability()` whenever `is_available()` says True. So once the skip on `test_fake_export` is removed, every XPU case dies at the `op_db` import in the child process before it reaches the op. `test_preserve_original_behavior` only passes because its first statement triggers init.

Setting both variables fixes this for me. An empty mask makes `_parse_visible_devices` return `[]`, so the count falls back to the SYCL runtime, which does respect the selector. That works, but it depends on a fallback path. It might be worth an issue that the count before init ignores `ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR`.

```python
def _get_env_by_device(device):
    device_type = torch.device(device).type
    if device_type == "cuda":
        return {"CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES": ""}
    if device_type == "xpu":
        return {**os.environ, "ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR": "*:cpu", "ZE_AFFINITY_MASK": ""}
    raise AssertionError(f"don't know how to hide {device_type} devices in a subprocess")
```

The `raise` covers the fallthrough. Right now any other device type gets `env={}`. That hides no device and also starts the child with an empty environment. So adding a backend to `only_for` would silently run the "simulated CPU machine" tests with the real device visible.
reviewer_principle: Hide devices consistently across initialization paths — Subprocess tests simulating no accelerator must configure both runtime selection and pre-initialization device discovery; for XPU this requires the SYCL selector and Level Zero affinity mask. Reject unsupported device types instead of silently running with visible hardware and an empty environment.
severity_reason: Detailed pre-init enumeration/import failure, verified source reports, and an explicit unsupported-device assertion.

## Summary
AOTAutograd metadata collection used to snapshot autocast dtype only for CUDA and CPU. The snapshot now walks `torch._C._autocast_supported_devices()` and records each device's autocast **dtype**.
During `run_functionalized_fw_and_collect_metadata`:
- Compare dtypes after the traced forward (inside `ExcludeDispatchKeyGuard`).
- If any supported device's dtype changed, raise with a per-device diff.
- Always restore prior dtypes and autocast nesting via `_preserve_autocast_dtypes` / `_preserve_autocast_nesting`.
**Enabled-state mutations are not checked.** `ExcludeDispatchKeyGuard` restores autocast enabled TLS on exit.

**What this function means.** `tensor_has_dispatch` was added in #78972 (June 2022, "Make FakeTensors return meta within kernel invocation, add FakeTensor op tests"). Before that, the debug-only autograd asserts were skipped only when a Python dispatch mode was active (`torch_dispatch_set()`). That PR split the skip into two halves:

- `dispatch_mode_enabled()`: a **mode** will intercept this op.
